articles.title: Revie Sorey, Bears guard who blocked for Payton and dedicated his life to helping at-risk kids, dies at 73
articles.text:
Revie Sorey, Bears guard who blocked for Payton and dedicated his life to helping at-risk kids, dies at 73 - WBEZ Chicago
Revie Sorey during his career as a Bear that spanned from 1975 to 1983.
Bob Langer/Sun-Times file
Sports
Obituaries
Revie Sorey, Bears guard who blocked for Payton and dedicated his life to helping at-risk kids, dies at 73
After leading the way for Walter Payton, Mr. Sorey made it his mission to pave the way for thousands of children in Chicago to reach their potential.
By
Mitch Dudek
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Revie Sorey, the Chicago Bears offensive lineman who for nine seasons blocked for Walter Payton and went on to dedicate his life to helping Chicago’s disadvantaged youth, died Thursday. He was 73.
Mr. Sorey was drafted by the Bears in 1975 and spent his entire NFL career with them. He wore number 69 and was an integral member of the Bears’ offensive line, playing 109 games between 1975 and 1983 and earning All-NFC honors.
Bears fans remember Mr. Sorey (his name is pronounced like it rhymes with “Stevie Story”) as the 6-3, 280-pound graceful big man who helped clear a path on countless sweeps for Payton.
Chicago Sun-Times. | Bob Langer/Sun-Times archive
“Everybody talks about his great infectious smile and how everybody he met became his buddy, his friend and how he went out of his way to make people feel special and guide people through their lives,” said Anita Efron. She and her husband, Morton Efron, a Chicago attorney who represented Mr. Sorey after he graduated from college, were Mr. Sorey’s closest friends and chosen family.
“I am getting literally hundreds of texts and emails from people who Revie helped. He just wanted to uplift people and show them how they could soar and be their best self,” Anita Efron said. “Everybody has said that there’s a connection with the Bears getting that win on Thanksgiving, the day he died, and, yeah, I think so, too.”
Born in Brooklyn, New York, and raised in Bedford-Stuyvesant, he attended the University of Illinois, where he became a two-time All-Big Ten football selection and offensive captain.
Mr. Sorey, who played guard, was at Northwestern Memorial Hospital when he died, said Anita Efron.
“His heart just stopped. It was his time,” she said.
The Efrons also released a statement Friday announcing Mr. Sorey’s death and recounting details of his life.
Following his football career, Mr. Sorey devoted himself to creating opportunities for young people, eventually serving as director of educational services at Ada S. McKinley Community Services, a youth services organization at 1359 W. Washington Blvd.
He founded the Revie Sorey Trunk Scholarship Program with Anita Efron, ensuring that hundreds of first-generation college-bound Chicago students received trunks filled with everything from computers to bedding.
Mr. Sorey’s wife, Suzy O’Malley-Sorey, died of pancreatic cancer in 2011.
Following her death, and with his own health beginning to fail, Mr. Sorey moved from his home in Glen Ellyn to the Efron’s downtown home until a stroke in March 2012 left him unable to speak or walk and in need of around-the-clock care.
Mr. Sorey then moved into a room at the Warren Barr Pavilion rehabilitation facility on the North Side that the Efrons decorated with football memorabilia. Through lots of hard work and therapy, he regained limited use of speech. The Efrons and his old Bears teammates were frequent visitors.
A Sun-Times reporter was present in 2016 when ex-Bears teammates Tom Hicks, Brian Baschnagel and Bruce Herron, who served as unofficial team barber when he was with the Bears, stopped by to provide Mr. Sorey with a haircut and some company.
“He nicknamed himself Dr. Rock Hollywood,” Hicks said then. Hicks met Mr. Sorey when they were freshmen at Illinois. “He was a riot. He dressed like Sly Stone. He drove a white Thunderbird with Dr. Rock Hollywood written on the back. It had a big aerial TV antenna on top that wasn’t attached to anything.
“I don’t know how much he paid in parking tickets. He was always parked illegally. He would wear a suit and carry a briefcase to class and then sleep through the lecture.”
In 2016, five years after his wife died, Mr. Sorey suffered additional heartache when his son, Trace Sorey, died in an accidental drowning at a pool in Los Angeles. He was 24.
“It was a horrible, just horrible,” Anita Effron recalled.
Mr. Sorey, who’d been living most recently at The Clare, a senior living facility downtown, is also remembered for mentoring young athletes through the Revie Sorey All-Pro Football Camp, which he and Anita Efron ran for 27 years, teaching young people to grow both on and off the field.
He also hosted the Revie Sorey Racquetball Classic, raising funds for local charities while introducing the sport to a diverse audience.

articles.title: Chicago's winter overnight parking ban returns Tuesday night — with higher fees

Chicago's winter overnight parking ban returns Tuesday night — with higher fees - WBEZ Chicago
A winter parking ban sign.
Rich Hein/Sun-Times
Weather
Money
Chicago's winter overnight parking ban returns Tuesday night — with higher fees
The city is raising its minimum towing fee to $250 and doubling daily storage costs to $50 for drivers who violate the restrictions.
By
Misha Manjuran Oberoi
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Chicago drivers could wake up to at least $360 in fees if they park on the wrong streets overnight this winter. The city’s annual overnight parking ban begins Tuesday, restricting parking on 107 miles of major streets.
The ban is enforced from 3 a.m. to 7 a.m. every day from Dec. 1 through April 1, according to the Department of Streets and Sanitation.
Vehicles parked in violation of the ban will be towed, and the cost is up significantly from last winter. Owners will face a minimum towing fee of $250, up from $150 last year, a $60 ticket and a $50 daily storage fee, which has doubled from $25.
The fees had remained unchanged for more than a decade before January of this year, when the department first increased them. The higher rates now also apply to the winter overnight parking ban.
The city tows an average of 60 to 65 vehicles per night throughout the winter season for violations of the overnight parking ban, the department added.
Vehicles are towed to Pound 2 at 10301 S. Doty Ave. or Pound 6 at 701 N. Sacramento.
The overnight ban is separate from the city’s 2-inch snow parking ban, which applies to another 500 miles of main streets. That restriction can take effect whenever at least two inches of snow accumulate on the street, regardless of the time of day or date.
Drivers parked on affected streets during a snowstorm could receive a ticket or have their vehicles relocated to make way for snow-clearing operations.
The city has permanently posted signs across streets affected by the overnight ban. The Streets and Sanitation Department also distributes flyers on parked cars before the restrictions begin.
The restrictions were introduced after major snowstorms in 1967 and 1979 brought Chicago traffic to a standstill.
Drivers can check whether their street is affected by viewing the city’s parking ban map. To check if your car was towed, visit chicagoshovels.org, or call 311.

articles.title: Soul Train Awards show debuts in Chicago with Chance the Rapper, Common and Chaka Khan
articles.text:
Chance the Rapper, Chaka Khan and Common appear at Soul Train Awards' Chicago debut - WBEZ Chicago
Common presents Chaka Khan with the Classic Soul Honor at the Soul Train Awards, which taped in Chicago and aired on Nov. 27 on BET and CBS.
Paras Griffin/BET
Movies & TV
Music
Arts & Culture
Soul Train Awards show debuts in Chicago with Chance the Rapper, Common and Chaka Khan
The ceremony paid homage to Chicago talent, history and culture while spotlighting Black entertainment icons and rising stars alike. Here’s what happened on- and off-camera.
By
Erica Thompson
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
The Chicago debut of the Soul Train Awards aired on Friday, honoring local talent, history and culture both on- and off-camera in an entertaining show that celebrated Black music icons and platformed rising stars.
Hometown legend Chaka Khan received the Classic Soul Honor, while another native, actress LisaRaye McCoy, oozed ‘70s chic in a white, bell-bottomed pantsuit and afro. Chicago comedians DeRay Davis and Deon Cole cracked jokes as they presented awards.
The awards taped at the Harris Theatre for Music and Dance weeks before air, and the pre-recorded nature of the event meant that audiences got to see celebrities riff between segments. South Side rapper, actor and author Common, another presenter, delighted the crowd with a very brief freestyle before doing a second take of his speech. On another break, two audience members were invited onstage to show off some classic Chicago street dances.
Chance the Rapper presents an award at the Soul Train Awards, which taped in early November at the Harris Theater for Music and Dance.
Paras Griffin/BET
The city received plenty of praise, too. There were shout-outs about Harold’s Chicken, Lakeshore Drive and other Chicago staples from the famous guests and host Anthony Anderson.
In other words, BET President and West Side native Louis Carr delivered on his promise to bring “true Chicago flavor” to the ceremony. It was the first time the city hosted the event, despite being the birthplace of the classic “Soul Train” TV program..
“I love award shows, and for it to be in the city that I’m from and highlighting all of the things we have here to celebrate — I was floored,” said attendee Lauren Gaston, 39, of Bellwood, after the event. “We are truly the blueprint and all of the other cities just follow our lead.”
From left, Mickey Guyton, Brittney Spencer and Robert Randolph salute Dolly Parton at the Soul Train Awards.
Leon Bennett/BET
Before the cameras started rolling, celebrities walked the purple carpet outside of the venue and mingled in the hallways. To keep things confidential before air, staffers gave attendees Yondr pouches to lock up their phones, though most entered the theater without them. However, many stern warnings were issued to people brave enough to text during the show.
Mayor Brandon Johnson addressed the crowd, praising Chicago’s music history and the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections, which took place two days before the ceremony. (The “blue wave” was a popular topic among presenters and honorees at the event.)
Then, gospel giant Kirk Franklin opened the show with an enthusiastic performance that was crashed by Anthony Anderson. The comical bit set the tone for the fun and light-hearted evening; Anderson was a masterful host who kept everyone laughing. He teased both the audience and the celebrities, including Chicago actor Larenz Tate, whom he praised for his enduringly fresh-faced appearance.
They must be putting something in the Garrett Popcorn, Anderson reasoned.
Rising star JayDon (back center) shows off dynamic dance moves at the 2026 Soul Train Awards.
Leon Bennett/BET
Other Chicago businesses, such as Cleo’s Southern Cuisine, were promoted in a video segment by Chicago historian Shermann Dilla Thomas. He also gave a short lesson about some of the city’s famous residents.
Ironically, the show was light on awards, opting to recognize a handful of veterans and newcomers instead of presenting a long list of competitive categories. The two honors voted on by fans, R&B/Soul Song of the Year and New Spotify R&B X International Artist, were anticlimactic: Winners Tyla and Partynextdoor were not in attendance.
The real draw were standout performers such as Khan, R&B icon El DeBarge and Soul Personified honoree Durand Bernarr. Another highlight was a tribute to Dolly Parton, performed by steel guitarist Robert Randolph and country singers Mickey Guyton and Brittney Spencer. Up-and-comers, including JayDon, Jai’Len Josey and New Soul honoree Elmiene, also impressed.
Louis Carr, who will exit BET at the end of the year, said it was important to honor the “Soul Train” tradition of introducing new artists to the world.
“Some people may say, ‘Who’s that?’” he said in an interview with the Sun-Times. “But one thing they won’t say is that they can’t sing.”
Soul Personified honoree Durand Bernarr performs at the 2026 Soul Train Awards. “Representation matters,” he told the Sun-Times. “There is something about being acknowledged by our people. I’m proud of us, and I hope that I’m making us proud.”
Aaron J. Thornton/BET
Surprisingly, Khan was the only Chicagoan who performed. While the local audience enjoyed seeing familiar faces, like Chance the Rapper, as presenters, it would have been more thrilling to hear him rap.
Another glaring omission was the absence of “Soul Train” dancers at the venue, especially as some of the original performers are still alive. And the noticeable amount of empty seats indicated that the invite-only guest list could have been expanded.
Overall, the show was a hit with attendees such as Shavonne Worthy, 39, of Hillside.
“I loved it,” she said. “It’s so great to celebrate Black excellence, and I love just being in a room with powerful people who really want to thrive and succeed.”

By

[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]

Chicago Sun-Times readers shared memories of late Chicago Bears offensive lineman Revie Sorey, who helped pave the way for legendary running back Walter Payton. Here is what you told us, lightly edited.
“I got to meet him at an all-day charity event when I was a kid. The first Chicago Bears player I ever met in person. He was great to us that day, and I’ll never forget shaking his hand. Rest easy, sir.”
— Jerry LaBuy
“Lucky enough to meet this awesome human during his playing days. He couldn’t have been nicer to me or all the other fans that day. Rest easy, big fella.”
— Steve Medel Sr.
“Classic player; what a thrill to watch him and Noah Jackson pave the way for Walter (Payton). Prayers.”
— Philip Doherty
“I was fortunate to work for him at the Hammond Boys & Girls Club. He became a great mentor of mine, and he has always held a special place in my heart. It’s a sad day in my home.”
— Cathie Dull
“He and Noah Jackson came to my elementary school for an assembly. I can’t remember the purpose of the assembly, but the two put on a spectacular display of dunking basketballs on the 8-foot rims.”
— Chris Zima
“I remember meeting him in grade school. He was a down-to-earth guy and was in tune with all of us youngsters.” Prayers to his family.’
— Chris J Vieweg
“Revie’s racquetball tournaments were some of the largest racquetball tournaments played in Illinois. I was fortunate to play with him and against him in a few tournaments. My son also went to Revie’s football camps. Rest in peace, Revie.”
— Patrice Marie
“Just saw this. Linemen for life. He and Noah Jackson were part of our childhood in the 70s.”
— Steven Henkel

articles.title: How a city program to help Chicago's blighted neighborhoods has fallen short
articles.text:
Chicago's TIF program to help blighted neighborhoods has fallen short on the West Side - WBEZ Chicago
The Downtown skyline seen from a former Sears facility on the West Side.
Joshua Lott | The New York Times
Nation/World
Politics
Neighborhoods
How a city program to help Chicago's blighted neighborhoods has fallen short
City Hall’s tax-increment financing program helped transform Downtown but has left some poorer neighborhoods including North Lawndale, East Garfield Park and West Garfield Park overlooked and neglected.
By
Nell Salzman | The New York Times
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Sears, Roebuck and Co. once employed thousands of workers at a 40-acre plant on the West Side where it produced the thick mail-order catalogs sent to homes across America.
Today, the former Sears facility looms over vacant lots and boarded-up churches, the hollowed-out skyline of a neighborhood that has been waiting for a comeback promised long ago by city officials.
About five miles east, in Downtown Chicago, a city tax-diversion program intended to revitalize blighted neighborhoods has helped stimulate employment and fund the development of gleaming skyscrapers, luxury housing and parks.
But on the West Side, where decades of underinvestment and rising costs have contributed to entrenched poverty, it has largely failed, The New York Times has found. That’s in part because of shifting political priorities and fractured oversight by city agencies of the tax-increment financing program, or TIF.
The disparity has long been apparent to people who live on the West Side, where many say their neighborhoods have been neglected for years and that grocery stores, new schools and job opportunities remain scarce.
The TIF program is under debate as Mayor Brandon Johnson says he is trying to prioritize funding for low-income neighborhoods.
Mayor Brandon Johnson (center) in October marking the completion of seven two-unit housing complexes in North Lawndale that were subsidized by a bond program that can use expired TIF funds.
Joshua Lott | The New York Times
A spokesman for the mayor said the city would keep working to “advance a more equitable vision for economic development, one that breaks from decades of uneven investment and puts public resources to work in the communities that need them most.”
The program is intended to jump-start public and private development in struggling areas. After the city draws a TIF district, tax revenue from rising property values within its borders is set aside to be reinvested in the area.
The Times compared projects in three of the poorest neighborhoods on the West Side — North Lawndale, East Garfield Park and West Garfield Park — to those in three similarly sized Downtown neighborhoods.
Over the past three decades, the TIF districts that included those downtown neighborhoods collected nearly $5 billion in revenue, more than double the $2 billion collected by the West Side districts.
Downtown, over $1 billion has been spent on projects, including affordable housing, a top program priority. Just over $100 million has been spent on such projects in the West Side neighborhoods.
Our examination focused on 16 housing developments in the three West Side neighborhoods.
One TIF redevelopment plan there projected increases in property values assuming the renovation of 1,000 residential units by 2036. The plan, created in 2000, was amended in 2015 to enlarge the project and extend its deadline.
The success of the TIF program that’s been seen Downtown hasn’t fully reached the West Side.
Josh Lott | The New York Times
Only about 400 units in fewer than 20 buildings in that area have been renovated so far, according to records from the city’s housing, planning and development agencies. Despite renovation, most of the buildings still have structural and maintenance problems, records show, including collapsing ceilings and broken windows.
New construction has been slow as well. Across the three West Side neighborhoods, about 700 housing units in roughly 40 new buildings went up, in part with TIF money, far short of satisfying housing needs. At one of those developments, construction costs rose to nearly $1 million per unit.
Thomas Cheatham, who lives in one of the new buildings, appreciates his spacious and sunlit apartment. But he said the area, with its empty storefronts and drug dealers, makes him wary of letting his children play outside.
TIF alone likely wasn’t going to solve deep, historical disparities on the West Side, and individual successes — a housing complex here, a store there — are not enough to transform a neighborhood like North Lawndale, where Cheatham lives. For years, the city has produced annual TIF reports detailing the finances of districts. Still, information on overall progress is fragmented across various agencies, making it difficult to track growth.
Thomas Cheatham lives in a new, mixed-income building on the West Side but says he rarely lets his young children go outside to play, citing the safety of the surrounding area.
Joshua Lott | The New York Times
David Doig, a TIF supporter who was the city’s planning and development commissioner under then-Mayor Richard M. Daley in the 1990s, said that, in the early years of the program, there was “much more emphasis on getting the deal done than there was on monitoring and compliance.”
TIF projects are supposed to provide a public benefit, like housing or jobs. In 2020, the city outlined a process for determining whether a project met that standard. But, according to 10 current and former officials, the city lacks the administrative capacity to adequately track, in real time, whether projects deliver.
Jim Horan, who was deputy commissioner in the housing and planning departments before retiring in 2024, said that, in recent years, the city’s management of projects has improved.
“Before, we just kind of accepted what developers came to us with,”

articles.title: Black Friday still brings animal-loving volunteers to Chicago stores in the spirit of giving
articles.text:
Black Friday still brings animal-loving volunteers to Chicago stores in the spirit of giving - WBEZ Chicago
Kim Riley, a volunteer with Felines & Canines, holds a toy for Ruby outside Menards in Lincoln Park, Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
Communities
Neighborhoods
Black Friday still brings animal-loving volunteers to Chicago stores in the spirit of giving
As crowds shrink and more shoppers turn to online deals, animal shelter volunteers are keeping a Black Friday tradition alive — stocking up on blankets, toys and treats for pets in need.
By
Christiana Freitag
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
At Menards in Lincoln Park, the busiest aisle on Black Friday wasn’t filled with shoppers hunting for electronics or holiday gifts. It was the one stacked with $1.50 blankets.
“You save big money at Menards,” Marie Kukielka said. “I don’t think I’ve ever been able to find a cheaper blanket.”
Kulkielka is among volunteers from no-kill animal shelters like PAWS Chicago and Canines & Felines Rescue who cross paths once a year at Menards, filling shopping carts with blankets, toys and treats for animals awaiting adoption.
For the volunteers, the annual shopping trip is less about scoring deals for themselves than giving back.
Kukielka said she began volunteering for PAWS after moving to Chicago to attend DePaul University, just a few blocks from the shelter. She had been Black Friday shopping since childhood, but eventually decided to redirect that enthusiasm toward something more meaningful.
“I still want to go, but maybe I should channel that energy into something a little bit better than just buying stuff I don’t need,” she said.
Carts full of dog supplies for PAWS Chicago are parked outside Menards in Lincoln Park, Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
Kukielka was joined by Erica Kazimir, another PAWS Chicago volunteer, who loaded about half a dozen carts with more than 200 blankets and toys and 100 bags of treats. The haul was just the first stop of the day, with trips to Target, Aldi and HomeGoods still ahead. They purchased 75 towels, 500 toys, 100 blocks of cream cheese and 60 jars of peanut butter by the end of the shopping day.
The two have been making the Black Friday rounds for PAWS for over a decade. Kazimir said the crowds have thinned considerably since the pandemic, making it easier for them to get in and out quickly.
“It was a little more cutthroat back then,” she said. “People would think our carts were part of the blanket bins and start taking blankets off.”
Retail experts predicted more shoppers would head online this year than to stores this Black Friday, according to a November survey by the National Retail Federation, with 89 percent of shoppers expected to shop online. Overall, the number of shoppers over the Thanksgiving weekend was anticipated to fall by 2.2 percent from last year, the NRF report found.
But volunteer shoppers like Kazimir are still showing up in person. Now, she said, volunteers from other shelters have become familiar faces in the aisles, returning year after year to shop for those in need.
“I’ve seen other shelters coming for the blankets, which is cool,” she said.
Erica Kazimir, left, and Marie Kukielka, volunteers at PAWS Chicago, load bags full of dog supplies for PAWS Chicago outside Menards, Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
The supplies will go first to PAWS’ adoption center on North Clybourn Avenue, which is currently housing around 450 animals, Kukielka estimated, with additional donations going to its medical center in Little Village.
The holidays can be a particularly busy time for the shelter, she said, as foster families travel and animals temporarily return to the adoption center. The organization is also preparing for its holiday adoption events.
PAWS raised more than $4,000 for this year’s shopping trip, she said. Kukielka’s bill totaled $1,375.22, but she saved $551.62 through the store’s Black Friday discounts.
Behind them in the checkout line were Kim Riley and her mother, Nada, continuing a tradition of their own. For about 20 years, the mother-daughter duo has shopped Black Friday sales for Felines & Canines, an Edgewater-based no-kill animal shelter.
This year, they picked up 15 blankets and toys, accompanied by Ruby, a yellow Labrador puppy. She’s training to become a therapy dog at Our Lady of Guadalupe School in the South Shore neighborhood, where Riley recently became principal.
For Riley, the early morning trip is worth it even on her days off.
“It’s really the only reason, aside from going to work this early, that I get up this early to go, if we can help some animals,” she said. “The point is to give. And if we have the means, we’re happy to share it.”
As shoppers increasingly turn to online deals and Black Friday crowds lose some of their traditional frenzy, the volunteers said the annual trips remain an opportunity to stretch donations and support Chicago’s animal shelters.
“That’s where everybody was today, all by the blankets,” Riley said. “There were so many people doing the same thing, which was really great.”
Kim Riley, a volunteer with Felines & Canines, holds Ruby for a photo outside Menards in Lincoln Park, Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times

articles.title: Grammy nominee Lil’ Ed Williams is carrying the Chicago blues tradition forward
articles.text:
Grammy nominee Lil’ Ed Williams is carrying the Chicago blues tradition forward - WBEZ Chicago
Blues guitarist and singer Lil’ Ed Williams has earned his first Grammy Award nomination for Best Traditional Blues Album.
Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
Music
Arts & Culture
Grammy nominee Lil’ Ed Williams is carrying the Chicago blues tradition forward
After decades in the business, the high-energy, slide guitar-shredding Williams, 71, has been nominated for his first Grammy.
By
Courtney Kueppers
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
When the 2027 Grammy nominations were announced earlier this month, several Chicagoans were on the list. But perhaps most underrated is local blues artist Lil’ Ed Williams, who earned his first Grammy nod at age 71.
Williams’ sound is pure Blues.  It’s all slide guitar and raw emotion. As he told me earlier this year, in this genre, there’s no faking it.
Green Room Newsletter

“See the thing about blues is you can’t change it because it’s part of you, it’s part of your lifeline. It’s your sadness, your happiness, it’s your crying, it’s your laughter. It’s a part of your body, it’s part of your soul,” Williams said in the spring, at the Alligator Records headquarters on Devon Avenue.
The local label, started by producer Bruce Iglauer, is celebrating its 55th anniversary this year. And Williams has been there for almost all of it. He’s now the label’s most senior artist.
“When I met Bruce, we kind of hit it off right off the bat. See, my dad left me when I was 6 years old. He left my house and he said, ‘I’ll see you next weekend,’ and I never seen him again. So Bruce was like my long-lost dad,” Williams said of Iglauer, who is now 79.
Alligator Records founder Bruce Iglauer met Williams at B.L.U.E.S. on Halsted in the 1980s. Since then, Williams has made 10 albums with the label.
Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
Williams, a West Side native, started playing music as a kid with a guitar given to him by his uncle, the Blues Hall of Famer, J.B. Hutto. Hutto won a Grammy for best traditional blues recording in 1985.
Now, Williams has a Grammy nomination of his own.
He and his band, the Blues Imperials, are up for best traditional blues album for their latest release, “Slideways.” Williams’ particular gift is the slide guitar, that high-energy, bold sound that emulates artists like Hound Dog Taylor.
That classic blues style is what Iglauer has liked about Williams’ music from day one. The musician and producer met at B.L.U.E.S. on Halsted, one of the Chicago clubs where Williams cut his teeth. Iglauer asked Williams and his band if they’d want to record a few songs for an upcoming Alligator compilation record.
“I was just going to record a couple of songs,” Iglauer remembered. “And I had a four-hour session booked, and they were done in an hour. And I said, in one of the most fateful phrases that I’ve ever used, ‘Would you like to do a few more?’ By the end of the evening we had cut 30 songs, and we had a debut album.”
Forty years and 10 albums later, Williams has his first Grammy recognition.
Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.
